claims.text: Severe plastic deformation followed by graded annealing will produce a controlled gradient in grain size and phase distribution.
High-strain-rate rolling will refine the alloy microstructure.
The resulting gradient microstructure will contain a fine-grained zone adjoining a coarser-grained core.
The fine-grained zone will enhance yield strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
The coarser-grained core will promote ductility.
The gradient structure will facilitate strain accommodation across the microstructure.
Controlled secondary-phase distributions will improve elastic stiffness.
Controlled secondary-phase distributions will increase resistance to crack propagation.
The proposed processing route will simultaneously enhance strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
Each of strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance is expected to improve by approximately 15–20% relative to standard homogenization and conventional thermomechanical treatments.
Conventionally processed high-entropy alloys typically exhibit a trade-off between strength and ductility.
Conventional treatments do not concurrently maximize elastic modulus and fracture resistance.
Successful performance requires precise control of deformation strain rate, annealing temperatures, and annealing times.
The approach is expected to work only when the alloy supports stable gradient-microstructure formation under the processing conditions.
Formation of unwanted brittle phases may negate the proposed improvements.
Excessive anisotropy may negate the proposed improvements.
The magnitude of improvement and its generalizability across alloy systems remain uncertain pending experimental validation.
